---
title: "F5 · The optimisation playbook"
description: "Twenty techniques, O1 to O20, that do almost all the work of making GenAI systems cheaper and faster. Chapters cite them by code."
---

The same twenty techniques do almost all of the cost and latency work in almost every system in
this book. This chapter describes each one once. System chapters cite them by code and give the
saving for that system, so you can see which techniques matter where.

O1 to O11 reduce the tokens you pay for, and apply whether you use an API or your own GPUs.
O12 to O20 make each GPU produce more tokens, and apply only when you self-host.

## Measure first

Before optimising, attribute cost. Tag every model call with the feature, the tenant and the step
that made it, and log the token counts the API returns. Then sort. Often one or two
steps account for most of the bill, and the right optimisation is obvious once you see which.
Without attribution it is easy to spend a sprint shortening a prompt that turns out to be 3% of the
cost.

## The catalogue

| Code | Technique | What it saves, and in proportion to what | Effort | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| <span class="ocode">O1</span> | Prompt caching | The cached prefix bills at the cache-read price (2.5% to 10% of input, by model) instead of the input price | Low | Silent cache misses |
| <span class="ocode">O2</span> | Retrieval budget and reranking | Input tokens, in proportion to the passages you stop sending | Medium | Lower recall |
| <span class="ocode">O3</span> | History compaction | Turns quadratic growth into linear | Medium | Lost context |
| <span class="ocode">O4</span> | Output control | Output tokens and decode time, in proportion | Low | Answers too terse |
| <span class="ocode">O5</span> | Tool definition trimming and tool search | The tokens of every definition removed, on every call | Low | The right tool is not found |
| <span class="ocode">O6</span> | Compact formats | Tokens on structured context; count them on your own data | Low | Model misreads the format |
| <span class="ocode">O7</span> | Batch APIs | 50% of model cost on anything not interactive, at current list prices | Low | Hours of latency |
| <span class="ocode">O8</span> | Response and semantic caching | The whole call on each hit; the hit rate comes from your logs | Medium | Wrong answer served from cache |
| <span class="ocode">O9</span> | Routing and cascades | The price gap between tiers, on the share routed down | Medium | Hard requests routed to weak models |
| <span class="ocode">O10</span> | Distillation and fine-tuning a small model | The price gap between large and small, minus training and serving | High | Quality drift, maintenance |
| <span class="ocode">O11</span> | Reasoning effort control | Thinking tokens on routes that do not need them | Low | Hard requests under-thought |
| <span class="ocode">O12</span> | Continuous batching | One read of the weights shared by every sequence in the batch | Low (built into servers) | None worth naming |
| <span class="ocode">O13</span> | Quantisation | Half or a quarter of the weight memory | Low to medium | Task-specific quality loss |
| <span class="ocode">O14</span> | Prefix caching on your own servers | Prefill on shared prefixes | Low | Memory pressure |
| <span class="ocode">O15</span> | Speculative decoding | Decode steps, in proportion to accepted draft tokens | Medium | Gain depends on acceptance rate |
| <span class="ocode">O16</span> | KV cache management | More concurrent sequences per GPU | Low | Preemption under load |
| <span class="ocode">O17</span> | Choosing the parallelism | Communication overhead per token | Medium | Wrong choice for the traffic |
| <span class="ocode">O18</span> | Chunked prefill and disaggregation | Stable inter-token latency under mixed load | Medium to high | Operational complexity |
| <span class="ocode">O19</span> | Autoscaling, spot and scale to zero | Pay for the average, not the peak | Medium | Cold starts of minutes |
| <span class="ocode">O20</span> | Right-sizing the hardware | The price gap between GPUs, if the smaller one meets the latency target | Low | Running out of headroom |

None of these is a measured saving. The column says what each technique removes and what the saving
is proportional to; each system chapter computes the figure for its own numbers, and the size of
anything that depends on quality or hit rates is something to measure.

## Token optimisation: O1 to O11

### O1 Prompt caching {#o1}

Providers can cache the processed form of a prompt prefix and reuse it on later requests that
start with exactly the same bytes. Cached tokens are billed at a small fraction of the input price,
and the first token arrives sooner because the prefix is not recomputed. Writing to the cache costs
a premium on the first request.

{{< include ../_generated/costs/f-cache-breakeven.md >}}

: Cost of a shared prefix over 10 requests within the cache lifetime, as a multiple of the uncached input price.

With a 5-minute lifetime, caching pays from the second request. The design rule that follows is to
**order prompts from most stable to least stable**: tool definitions, then the system prompt, then
long reference documents, then conversation history, then the new message. Anything that varies per
request (a timestamp, a user ID, a randomly ordered list) placed early in the prompt breaks the
cache for everything after it. Check the cache-read count the API returns; if it is zero on
repeated requests, something early in the prompt is changing.

Three details catch people. There is a minimum prefix length below which nothing is cached, and
a shorter prompt is processed uncached without an error. On Claude it is 512 tokens for the 5.5
models, Opus 5, Fable and Mythos; 1,024 for Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.8; and up to 4,096 for older
models such as Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic's prompt caching documentation, checked 2026-11-04). Caches
belong to one model, so routing a conversation between two models forfeits the cache on each switch. And the cache
lifetime counts from the start of the request, so slow, bursty traffic may need the longer
lifetime option, which costs more to write.

### O2 Retrieval budget and reranking {#o2}

In retrieval systems, the retrieved passages are usually most of the input. Retrieving twenty
passages to be safe and sending all of them costs four times as much as sending five, and gives
the model fifteen more passages to ignore, which can make answers worse; measure answers, not just
recall. Retrieve wide (20 to 50 candidates), rerank with a cross-encoder, and send the top 3 to 8.
Rerankers are priced per token, so whether reranking pays for itself in generation tokens depends on
the generator's price: with a mid-tier or larger model the passages it removes cost more than the
reranking, and with the cheapest models they can cost less, so reranking has to earn its place on
quality instead ([System 8](../systems/08-production-rag.qmd) works through both).

### O3 History compaction {#o3}

A conversation re-sends its whole history on every turn. With a fixed prefix of $s$ tokens and
$g$ tokens added per turn, the total input over $n$ turns is

$$
n \cdot s + g \cdot \frac{n(n-1)}{2}
$$

which grows with the square of the number of turns. A 30-turn agent session that adds 2,000 tokens
per turn sends about 870,000 history tokens in total. Fixes, in order of preference: cache the
history (<span class="ocode">O1</span>) so most of it bills at the read price; drop or truncate
old tool results, which are usually the bulk; and summarise older turns into a short state once
the history passes a threshold.

### O4 Output control {#o4}

Output tokens cost {{< var f.ratio.out_in_low >}} to {{< var f.ratio.out_in_high >}} times as
much as input tokens on the current models and determine decode time. Ask for the
format you need and no more: a JSON object instead of prose, bullet points instead of paragraphs,
"answer in at most three sentences". Use structured output modes where the API offers them, both
to save tokens and to remove retry loops caused by malformed output. Set `max_tokens` to a hard
ceiling that matches the format, as a guard rather than as the main control.

### O5 Tool definition trimming and tool search {#o5}

Every tool definition is sent with every request. Fifty tools at 300 tokens each is 15,000 tokens
before the conversation starts. Remove tools the current step cannot use, shorten descriptions
to what the model needs to choose correctly, and for large tool sets use a tool search mechanism
that loads definitions on demand. Keep the tool list deterministic in order, or it breaks the
prompt cache.

### O6 Compact formats {#o6}

The same table costs 20% to 40% fewer tokens as CSV or a Markdown table than as JSON with
repeated keys. Replace long URLs and UUIDs with short local references and map them back after
the call. Strip boilerplate (navigation, footers, signatures) from documents before they reach
the prompt. Check on the golden set that the model reads the compact form as well as the verbose
one.

### O7 Batch APIs {#o7}

The major providers in the price table run submitted jobs asynchronously at half price, within a
completion window of up to 24 hours. Anything not waiting on a person belongs here: nightly summaries,
backfills, evaluations, post-call analytics, catalogue generation. It is the cheapest saving in
the book, and the most often forgotten.

### O8 Response and semantic caching {#o8}

Store final answers keyed by the request. An exact-match cache is safe and useful for repeated
identical requests. A semantic cache matches requests by embedding similarity, so "how many
leave days do I get" can hit an entry stored for "what is my annual leave allowance". The hit rate
depends entirely on how repetitive the traffic is: expect almost nothing for open-ended chat and
more for narrow FAQ-style traffic, but estimate it from your own logs before building one. Replay a
month of questions in order and count those with an earlier question above your similarity
threshold whose source documents have not changed since; that count is the hit rate. The
risk is serving a cached answer to a question that only looked similar, or serving an answer whose
source has changed. Key entries by the source documents they used and invalidate on change, set a
strict similarity threshold, and never semantically cache anything personalised.

### O9 Routing and cascades {#o9}

Send each request to the cheapest model that handles it. A **router** decides up front, using
rules or a small classifier. A **cascade** tries the cheap model first and escalates when a check
fails (low confidence, failed validation). Both save the most when traffic is skewed towards easy
requests; count the share in your own logs. Measure the simpler option first: one model with
per-route effort (<span class="ocode">O11</span>) may match a router at lower complexity, and it
keeps one cache.

### O10 Distillation and fine-tuning a small model {#o10}

For a narrow, high-volume task (classify this ticket, extract these ten fields) a small model
fine-tuned on outputs from a large one may match the large model on that task. The price gap
between the two is the ceiling on the saving, and the golden set decides whether you get it. The
large model labels a few thousand examples; the small one learns them. It is potentially the
largest single saving and the most work: you now own a training pipeline, an evaluation gate and a
model that drifts as your data does.

### O11 Reasoning effort control {#o11}

Thinking tokens are billed as output. Setting effort low on routes that do not need deep
reasoning (chat, extraction, formatting) cuts the thinking tokens on those routes, and setting it high only
where evaluations show it helps keeps quality where it matters. Tune it per route, measured on the
golden set, and judge the result by cost per completed task: a cheaper call that needs a retry is
not cheaper.

## Inference optimisation: O12 to O20

These apply when you serve models on your own GPUs. [System 39](../systems/39-self-hosted-inference.qmd)
uses all of them.

### O12 Continuous batching {#o12}

Decoding one token reads every weight from memory (see [F2](f2-numbers.qmd)). Serving sequences
one at a time wastes almost all of the GPU. Continuous batching adds new sequences to the running
batch at every step and removes finished ones, so the GPU always works on as many sequences as
memory allows. Every serious inference server (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, TGI) does it by
default. The thing to tune is the maximum batch size, which trades per-stream speed against total
throughput.

### O13 Quantisation {#o13}

Store weights in fewer bits. FP8 halves weight memory relative to 16-bit, and Hopper and later
GPUs compute in FP8 natively. The quality loss is model- and task-specific. 4-bit formats (AWQ, GPTQ, and the MX formats)
quarter memory and fit large models on fewer GPUs, with more risk. Less memory for weights means
more for the KV cache, so quantisation raises throughput as well as cutting the GPU count. Always
re-run your own evaluation after quantising; losses concentrate in specific skills (arithmetic,
long-context recall, non-English text) that average benchmarks hide.

### O14 Prefix caching on your own servers {#o14}

The self-hosted version of <span class="ocode">O1</span>. The server keeps KV cache blocks for
prefixes it has seen and reuses them. With a shared system prompt, few-shot examples or a common
document, most of the prefill disappears. Route requests that share a prefix to the same replica
(prefix-aware load balancing) or each replica rebuilds the same cache.

### O15 Speculative decoding {#o15}

A cheap draft (a small model, extra prediction heads, or n-gram lookup from the prompt) proposes
several tokens, and the large model verifies them in one forward pass. Accepted tokens are free
decode steps. The gain depends on two things: the share of drafted tokens the large model
accepts, which is higher when output is predictable (code edits, extraction that copies from the
input), and how much the extra verified tokens add to each step's cost.
[System 39](../systems/39-self-hosted-inference.qmd) works out the acceptance rate needed to break
even.

### O16 KV cache management {#o16}

Paged KV storage (introduced by vLLM as PagedAttention) allocates the cache in blocks, so memory
is not reserved for the maximum length of every sequence. Storing the KV cache in FP8 halves it
again. Offloading cold cache blocks to CPU memory or local disk keeps long shared prefixes
available without holding GPU memory. Watch the cache utilisation metric: near 100% means new
requests wait or running ones are preempted and recomputed.

### O17 Choosing the parallelism {#o17}

A model that does not fit on one GPU is split across several with tensor parallelism. Splitting
further than needed adds communication and lowers throughput per GPU. For a given number of GPUs,
compare few large replicas against many small ones: more replicas avoid communication overhead,
and wider replicas split each step across more GPUs. Which wins on total throughput and on latency
per stream depends on the model and the traffic, so measure both. Mixture-of-experts models add
expert parallelism, and their decode cost follows the active parameters, not the total.

### O18 Chunked prefill and disaggregation {#o18}

A long prompt's prefill can occupy the GPU for hundreds of milliseconds and stall every stream that
is decoding. Chunked prefill splits it and interleaves it with decode steps, which keeps
inter-token latency stable. At larger scale, disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on
separate GPU pools and moves the KV cache between them, so each pool can be sized and tuned for
its own bottleneck. In this book's judgement it earns its complexity only at many nodes.

### O19 Autoscaling, spot and scale to zero {#o19}

GPU nodes take minutes to start and load weights, so scale on leading signals (queue depth, KV
cache utilisation, waiting requests) rather than on CPU. Keep a reserved base for the steady load,
burst on demand for the peaks, and run batch work on spot capacity that can be interrupted. Models
with little traffic should scale to zero or move to an API.

### O20 Right-sizing the hardware {#o20}

An 8B model may not need an H100. One H100 on AWS costs {{< var f.f5.h100_gpu_hour >}} a GPU-hour
inside a p5.48xlarge, against {{< var f.f5.l4_hour >}} for one L4 (g6.xlarge), a factor of
{{< var f.f5.h100_l4_ratio >}}. Whether the smaller GPU meets your latency target is a load test;
if it does, that price gap is the saving. Match the GPU to the model size and the latency target, and
check the price per GPU-hour across providers: the same H100 costs very different amounts on
different clouds (see [Prices](../appendix/prices.qmd)).

## The order to apply them

1. Attribute cost, so you know where the money goes.
2. Apply the free ones: <span class="ocode">O4</span> output control, <span class="ocode">O1</span>
   caching, <span class="ocode">O11</span> effort, <span class="ocode">O5</span> tools,
   <span class="ocode">O2</span> retrieval budget.
3. Move everything non-interactive to batch, <span class="ocode">O7</span>.
4. Only then trade quality risk for cost: <span class="ocode">O9</span> routing,
   <span class="ocode">O8</span> semantic caching, <span class="ocode">O10</span> distillation.
5. Self-host, with <span class="ocode">O12</span> to <span class="ocode">O20</span>, when the
   arithmetic in System 39 says the volume justifies it.
